title: Performance: where compiled code wins and how it was measured
summary: Gains come from not tokenising, direct calls and the IBM REXX/370 compiler's techniques (Tom Dyer's brief): stems as arrays, machine-integer loop counters and operators, native registers. Tight-loop bench native/bench/loops.rex: 4.49 s to 0.26 s compiled against 1.55 s interpreted. The compiler compiling itself: native 250 s, interpreted 344 s (fixed point at cd77a49). Josep Maria Blasco's Rexx Parser benchmark (pbench2.rex), merge gate of main d43c058 (2026-10-27): three passes 38.0 s compiled against 117.5 s interpreted (3.09x), dumps identical over 162,260 elements, 71,087 trips to the interpreter a pass, peak 315 MB (the interpreter: 379 MB). HANDOFF sections 'The cycle collector and the Rexx Parser' and 'Call-path costs' record how (a leak closed, 80.1 G to 65.6 G instructions a pass). rexxcps (string work) is still slower compiled than the Release interpreter: 7.79 G against 5.16 G instructions; Value copies are most of the gap. Crossings (calls between compiled code and the interpreter) can dominate when compiled code works on interpreter objects, but on pbench2 they are about 1%: count and sample before optimising.
invariants: Every fast path keeps the interpreter's results byte for byte; it checks its case at run time and otherwise falls back.
Time on an idle machine, one build or run at a time; report interpreted and compiled side by side.
Report numbers with the commit they were measured on.

A trip to the interpreter (a message to an interpreter object) costs about 2.3 us from compiled code against under 1 us inside the interpreter: each API call takes the kernel lock. Read String results in place (stringFields), never add API calls to a hot path, count trips with RX2CPP_BIF_STATS=1.

When sampling shows no hotspot, use callgrind (valgrind --tool=callgrind; callgrind_annotate --tree=caller) on one pass: instruction counts are exact and unaffected by load, and the caller tree shows where a flat cost comes from.
